title: College Is Not a Rite of Passage
author: mperrone
summary: The mperrone newsletter uses Aaron Renn's insight about society's competing 'playbooks' to argue that college has been treated as a rite of passage -- a transitional ceremony that marks adult membership -- while marriage, which is the institution that actually requires community investment and intergenerational transmission to sustain, has been progressively stripped of its communal infrastructure. The piece argues that college succeeds as a rite of passage because it has institutions (universities), a clear sequence (four years), a defined outcome (degree), and a supporting community (campus). Marriage has none of these: it is presented as a personal decision between two people, with almost no institutional support, no structured preparation, and increasingly no communal expectation that it is the default path to adult flourishing. The piece argues that reversing the cultural decline of marriage requires not individual moral persuasion but communal infrastructure: mentorship, preparation, ceremony, and the explicit transmission of the belief that marriage is worth building a life around.
points: * College succeeds as a rite of passage because it has institutional infrastructure: a defined sequence, a clear outcome, and a supporting community that sustains the participant through the transition. * Marriage has been stripped of its communal infrastructure: it is presented as a private decision between two individuals with no structured preparation, no institutional support, and diminishing communal expectation that it is the normal adult path. * Reversing the cultural decline of marriage requires communal infrastructure, not individual moral persuasion: mentorship programs, structured preparation, explicit transmission of the belief that marriage is worth building a life around. * The 'playbook' concept (from Aaron Renn) explains why marriage rates are declining: the college playbook is legible, supported, and resourced; the marriage playbook has become illegible, unsupported, and under-resourced. * The piece's most sobering observation is that the communities best positioned to rebuild the marriage playbook -- religious congregations with the relational density and shared values required -- have largely retreated from the explicit transmission of marriage culture.
quotes: College is a rite of passage. Not because a degree is meaningful -- it may or may not be -- but because the institutional infrastructure around college does exactly what rites of passage are supposed to do: it takes you from one stage of life to another, through a defined sequence, with a community watching and supporting the transition.

Marriage used to have that infrastructure. It had pre-marital preparation (formal and informal), mentorship from married adults in the community, ceremony that broadcast the transition publicly, and an ongoing communal investment in the success of the new household. Most of that is gone.

Aaron Renn's insight about 'playbooks' is exactly right here. The college playbook is legible. Everybody knows it. You graduate high school, you go to college for four years, you get a degree, you enter the workforce. The steps are clear, the supports are in place, the community celebrates each milestone. The marriage playbook has become illegible.

What would it take to rebuild the marriage playbook? Not sermons. Not moral condemnation of people who choose differently. Infrastructure. Structured mentorship from happily married couples to engaged couples. Preparation programs that actually work. Communities that explicitly celebrate and support marriage formation as a communal good.

The communities best positioned to build this infrastructure are religious congregations -- they have the relational density, the shared values, and the intergenerational presence that secular institutions cannot replicate. The question is whether they will treat marriage formation as a mission rather than an assumption.
